details:
**The Birth of Venus**
Botticelli's most famous painting (c. 1485, Uffizi, Florence), in tempera on canvas. The nude goddess Venus stands in a modest pose on a giant scallop shell, covering herself with her long red-gold hair, while the wind god Zephyrus, embracing Chloris, blows her to shore amid falling roses. On the right, a Hora (a goddess of the seasons) rushes to cover her with a flowered cloak.

**Primavera**
Botticelli's allegory of spring (c. 1480, Uffizi), set in a dark orange grove. Venus stands in the center beneath a blindfolded Cupid, with the Three Graces dancing at the left, and at the right the blue-skinned Zephyrus seizes the nymph Chloris, who turns into Flora, the flower-strewn goddess of spring. The painting draws on Ovid's Fasti and the poetry of Poliziano.

**Zephyrus and Chloris**
The west wind and the nymph he pursued, who appear in both of Botticelli's great mythological paintings. In Primavera, the ghostly Zephyrus grabs Chloris, who is transformed into Flora; in The Birth of Venus, the two fly together, blowing Venus toward the shore.

**Mercury and his caduceus**
At the far left of Primavera, the messenger god Mercury, in a red cloak with a sword at his side, raises his caduceus (snake-entwined staff) to push away wispy clouds or reach toward the oranges. He is often seen as representing the month of May.

**Three Graces**
The trio of dancing goddesses at the left of Primavera, who hold hands in a circle and wear translucent white gowns. Cupid aims a flaming arrow at one of them from above.

**The Mystical Nativity**
Botticelli's late nativity (c. 1500, National Gallery, London), his only signed and dated work. A Greek inscription at the top refers to the Book of Revelation and the troubles of the time. Above the thatched stable, twelve angels in white, red, and green (the colors of faith, hope, and charity) dance in a circle holding olive branches, while in the foreground angels embrace men as small demons flee.

**Venus and Mars**
Botticelli's painting (c. 1485, National Gallery, London) of the goddess Venus, awake and alert, watching her lover Mars sleep. Mischievous baby satyrs play with Mars's lance and armor, one wears his helmet, and another blows a conch shell in his ear. Wasps buzz near Mars's head, possibly a pun on the Vespucci family name.

**Madonna of the Magnificat**
A Botticelli tondo (circular painting) in the Uffizi showing the Virgin Mary writing the Magnificat, her hymn of praise, in a book, as two angels hold a delicate golden crown over her head. The infant Christ guides her hand, and the Madonna may have been modeled on Lucrezia Tornabuoni.

**Madonna of the Pomegranate**
Another Botticelli tondo in the Uffizi, in which Mary holds the Christ Child, who holds a pomegranate, a symbol of the Passion and resurrection. Six angels surround them, and golden rays shine down from above.

**Sistine Chapel frescoes**
In 1481–1482, years before Michelangelo painted the ceiling, Botticelli was among the Florentine painters called to Rome to fresco the chapel's walls. His scenes include The Youth of Moses (Trials of Moses), The Temptations of Christ, and The Punishment of Korah.

**Girolamo Savonarola**
The Dominican friar whose apocalyptic preaching dominated Florence in the 1490s and led to the "Bonfire of the Vanities." Botticelli is said to have fallen under his influence, and his late works, like The Mystical Nativity, take on a more somber, religious tone.

**Adoration of the Magi**
Botticelli's painting (c. 1475, Uffizi) in which members of the Medici family, his chief patrons, appear as the three Magi and their attendants. Botticelli included a self-portrait at the far right, looking out at the viewer.

**Pallas and the Centaur**
A Botticelli painting (Uffizi) in which the goddess Pallas Athena, holding a large halberd (a battle-axe on a pole), grips the hair of a sheepish centaur. It is often read as wisdom or reason taming passion.

**The Calumny of Apelles**
A late Botticelli allegory (c. 1494, Uffizi) recreating a lost painting by the ancient Greek painter Apelles, as described by Lucian. A judge with donkey ears is advised by Ignorance and Suspicion, who pull at his ears and hair, while Calumny drags a victim by the hair before him, and the nude figure of Truth points up to heaven.

**Fra Filippo Lippi**
The Florentine painter who was Botticelli's teacher; his graceful, linear style shaped Botticelli's early Madonnas. Botticelli's other works include the fresco Saint Augustine in His Study, which shows the saint surrounded by books and an armillary sphere.
